evidence.excerpt:
As claims about recursive self-improvement (RSI) and artificial general intelli-
gence (AGI) proliferate, we ask a simple question: do frontier AI models have a
sense of data, i.e., can they reliably select the right data for training? We intro-
duce DataSense-Bench1 to study this capability through the fundamental problem
of data selection and performance forecasting in machine learning. We ask AI
agents to select and rank candidate training subsets that can be used to fine-tune a
small LLM model. Agents are allowed to inspect the data, write and execute anal-
ysis code, and run model forward passes, but can not train the model or access
the actual evaluation tasks. We then fine-tune the base model on each selected
subset and evaluate its post-training performance under a standardized protocol.
We instantiate the benchmark in terminal problem solving and tool use,

evidence.excerpt:
Anticipating which changes will improve a model can help recursive self-improvement allocate
training resources more effectively. As these systems take on research roles, data sense becomes a
concrete part of that challenge: connecting properties of training examples to what a model will learn
from them. We introduce DATASENSE-BENCHto evaluate this data sense through selecting useful
subsets and predicting their relative post-training performance. Across terminal problem solving and
multi-turn tool use, agents construct plausible, data-specific recipes, but selection gains over random
selection are limited. Agents do not reliably rank their selected groups, and this ability does not hold
consistently across tasks. These results highlight a gap between producing a convincing analysis of
data and making reliable decisions about its training value, motivating data sense as a capability

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Post-training performance is measured on held-out downstream benchmarks, TBLite automated verifiers and BFCL tool-execution checks, after fixed SFT runs.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Downstream task scores from TBLite verifiers and BFCL tool-use checks applied to fine-tuned checkpoints.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Agent-designed selection heuristics using structural features, base-model loss, and prompted quality judgments during data selection.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims match empirical results: agent data selection yielded modest gains over random subsets, agents often failed to accurately rank subset utility or reliably identify the optimal subset, and selection strategies lacked consistency across runs.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation covers multiple frontier agents across replicated runs, measuring downstream post-training performance, gains over random baselines, Spearman rank correlation, and top-group identification accuracy, with full trace logging and cost analyses.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Downstream test accuracy and reward scores on held-out benchmark tasks evaluated after independent SFT runs.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Downstream task execution benchmarks (TBLite automated verifiers and BFCL tool execution test suites) applied to checkpoints after fixed supervised fine-tuning.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Agent-designed heuristics, loss metrics, structural feature filters, and prompted quality scores used during data selection without training feedback.

primary.limitations: The work explicitly acknowledges its focus on SFT of existing trajectories, excluding reinforcement learning post-training or synthetic data generation, and notes variation in agent execution traces.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology strictly isolates data selection from evaluation: agents receive candidate pools, inference-only model access, and training configurations, producing frozen ranked subsets before models are fine-tuned via standardized supervised recipes and scored on independent downstream tasks.
primary.quality_rationale: The study presents a clear, well-scoped protocol with strong experimental design, thorough empirical evaluation of multiple models across diverse tasks, transparent error metrics, and disciplined interpretations avoiding overclaiming.
primary.scoped_contribution: DataSense-Bench, a benchmark assessing whether frontier CLI LLM agents can select and rank training data subsets for fine-tuning without observing post-training outcomes, instantiated on terminal problem-solving (TBLite) and tool-use (BFCL) tasks.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The study presents a clear, well-scoped protocol with strong experimental design, thorough empirical evaluation of multiple models across diverse tasks, transparent error metrics, and disciplined interpretations avoiding overclaiming.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The work explicitly acknowledges its focus on SFT of existing trajectories, excluding reinforcement learning post-training or synthetic data generation, and notes variation in agent execution traces.
